questions.question_text:
In a random sample of $600$ shoppers, $174$ used a loyalty card.
What is the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ of shoppers who used a loyalty card?

options.why: Used the $426$ shoppers who did not use a card, giving the proportion of failures instead of successes.
Gave the count $X$ rather than dividing it by $n$ to get a proportion.
Divided $n$ by $X$ instead of $X$ by $n$; a proportion can never exceed $1$.

questions.question_text:
In a large population, $28\%$ of trees are eucalypts.
A random sample of $750$ trees is taken and $\hat{p}$ is the proportion of eucalypts in the sample.
What is $E(\hat{p})$?

options.why: Gave $E(X)=np$, the expected number of eucalypts, instead of the expected proportion.
Gave $1-p$, the proportion of trees that are not eucalypts.
Divided $p$ by $n$; the division by $n$ belongs in the variance, not in the mean.
Used $np(1-p)$, which is the variance of the count $X$, not of the proportion $\hat{p}$.
Computed $p(1-p)$ but forgot to divide by $n$.
Gave the standard deviation $\sqrt{0.0004}$ instead of the variance.
Gave $\text{Var}(\hat{p})$ without taking the square root.
Computed $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$, the standard deviation of the count $X$, not of $\hat{p}$.
Took $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$ and left out the division by $n$.

questions.question_text:
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(2000,0.35)$ and $\hat{p}=\dfrac{X}{2000}$.
Which pair gives $E(\hat{p})$ and $\sigma(\hat{p})$, the standard deviation correct to four decimal places?

options.why: Gave the mean and standard deviation of the count $X$ rather than of the proportion.
Took the mean of $\hat{p}$ correctly but used $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$, the spread of the count.
Took the spread of $\hat{p}$ correctly but used $E(X)=np$ as the mean.

questions.question_text:
In a large population, $40\%$ of people own a bicycle.
A random sample of $2400$ people is taken.
What is the standard deviation of the sample proportion of bicycle owners, correct to four decimal places?

options.why: Gave the variance $0.0001$ without taking its square root.
Used $\sqrt{2400\times 0.4\times 0.6}$, the standard deviation of the count instead of the sample proportion.
Used $\sqrt{0.4\times 0.6}$, omitting the division by the sample size inside the square root.

questions.question_text:
In a large population, $60\%$ of members renew their subscription.
What is the smallest sample size $n$ for which $\sigma(\hat{p})<0.01$?

options.why: Allowed equality at $\sigma(\hat{p})=0.01$, although the question requires a strict inequality.
Used $0.01$ instead of $0.01^2$ after removing the square root, obtaining $n>24$.
Used $p^2=0.36$ instead of $p(1-p)=0.24$, obtaining $n>3600$.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{\dfrac{0.6\times 0.4}{n}}<0.01$
$\dfrac{0.24}{n}<0.0001$
$0.24<0.0001n$
$n>2400$
The smallest whole number greater than $2400$ is $2401$.

questions.question_text:
In a large population, $25\%$ of households own a dog.
What is the smallest sample size $n$ for which the standard deviation of the sample proportion of dog-owning households is less than $0.02$?

options.why: Rounded the boundary $468.75$ down, although $n$ must be greater than this boundary.
Used $0.02$ instead of $0.02^2$ after removing the square root, obtaining $n>9.375$.
Used $p^2=0.0625$ instead of $p(1-p)=0.1875$, obtaining $n>156.25$.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{\dfrac{0.25\times 0.75}{n}}<0.02$
$\dfrac{0.1875}{n}<0.0004$
$0.1875<0.0004n$
$n>468.75$
The smallest whole number greater than $468.75$ is $469$.
